readerTitle: Why Walmart sold a $1.5 billion business with no audit
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Berkshire Hathaway의 McLane 인수, Nebraska Furniture Mart 인수) + 가상 적용 (지역 도매상, 리모델링 업체)
insight: 평판은 협상 테이블에 나보다 먼저 도착한다. 정직은 이번 거래의 비용이 아니라 다음 모든 거래의 확인 비용, 보호 장치, 할인을 줄여 주는 자산이다.
misconception: 작은 허세나 거짓말은 이번 거래에만 영향을 준다. 협상에서 윤리를 지키면 돈을 손해 본다.

sources.text: Berkshire Hathaway 2003 Annual Letter to Shareholders (McLane 인수, 실사 없음, 29일)
Berkshire Hathaway 1983 Annual Letter to Shareholders (Nebraska Furniture Mart 인수)

factChecks.note: McLane 인수(2003년) 가격은 약 15억 달러로 알려져 있습니다. 2003년 서한의 정확한 금액과 "실사를 하지 않았다", "29일 만에 완료" 표현을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 직접 인용 없이 의역으로만 적었습니다.
Nebraska Furniture Mart 인수(1983년)가 악수와 짧은 계약서, 감사 없이 이뤄졌다는 내용은 여러 자료에 나오지만 세부("한 쪽짜리 계약서" 등)는 자료마다 다릅니다. 카드에는 "reportedly"로 일반적으로만 적었습니다.
7번 카드의 '거짓 사실 진술 금지' 원칙은 일반 원칙으로만 다뤘습니다. 국가별 계약법·사기 관련 법률 조언은 하지 않습니다.

cards.title: Why Walmart sold a $1.5 billion business with no audit
body: In 2003, Walmart sold McLane, its grocery and goods distribution arm, to Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway for about $1.5 billion.
Berkshire skipped the usual months of checking the books. The deal took 29 days. Buffett said he simply trusted that everything would be as Walmart described it.

image.label: A handshake over a stack of unopened files
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 회의 테이블 위에서 두 손이 악수하고, 옆에는 봉인된 채 열리지 않은 서류 상자 더미. 배경에 트럭과 물류 창고 실루엣. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The buyer asks about other offers.
body: You're selling a regional wholesale business. A serious buyer is close to a deal but asks: "Do you have other offers?" You don't.
What do you say?

options.text: "Yes, another buyer is interested," to push the price up
options.feedback: It might add a few percent today. If they ever learn it was false, they start doubting every number in your books, and that costs far more.

options.text: "I'd rather not discuss other talks. Here's why the price is fair."
options.feedback: You protect your position without saying anything false. Your figures keep their credibility, and that's what moves the price.

options.text: "No, you're the only one," and hope they reward the honesty
options.feedback: Honest, and it builds trust. But you've given away leverage you didn't need to give. Not lying is different from telling everything.

cards.title: Trust made the deal faster and simpler.
body: Big acquisitions usually mean teams of accountants and lawyers, long contracts and protections against hidden problems. All of that costs time and money.
Berkshire had done this before. In 1983 Buffett bought most of Nebraska Furniture Mart from its founder, Rose Blumkin, reportedly on a handshake and a short agreement, without an audit.
In both cases, the seller's record of keeping its word replaced much of the checking.

cards.title: Reputation is a negotiating asset.
body: Your **reputation** is what the other side believes about your word before you say anything.
When they trust it, they check less, ask for fewer guarantees and decide faster. When they doubt it, they protect themselves, and you pay for that protection.
So honesty is not just a moral choice that costs you at the table. It lowers the cost of every deal that comes after.

image.label: Two paths to a deal: short with trust, long with checks
image.brief: 두 갈래 길 인포그래픽. 위쪽 "Trusted" 길은 짧고 곧게 "Deal"에 도착. 아래쪽 "Doubted" 길은 "Audits", "Guarantees", "Delays", "Lower price" 표지판을 지나며 구불구불하게 돌아감.

cards.title: The trust tax
body: When the other side doubts you, they add costs to protect themselves:
list: **Tighter terms:** deposits, penalties, money held back until delivery
**A lower price:** a discount for the risk that you're not telling the truth
cards.callout: You pay this tax on every deal, not just the one where you bent the truth.

cards.title: Small markets have long memories.
body: Most industries are smaller than they look. Buyers, suppliers, lenders and staff move between firms and talk.
A lie that's caught doesn't stay inside one deal. It travels to people you haven't met yet, and it colors every claim you make, even the true ones.
cards.softwareNote: A common version: a sales rep promises a feature "coming next quarter" to close a contract. When it doesn't ship, the customer stops believing the roadmap, renewal talks get harder, and the story reaches other buyers through reviews and references.

cards.title: Honest doesn't mean telling everything.
body: You can keep your bottom line private, decline to answer, or say "I'd rather not share that." Good negotiators do this all the time.
The line is stating things you know are false: fake offers, hidden defects, made-up deadlines. That's where reputation breaks, and in some places it can also create legal risk.
And trust is earned slowly. One honest deal won't get you a no-audit handshake.

cards.title: Now you run a renovation company.
body: You're about to sign a kitchen remodel. You've just learned the cabinets you quoted will arrive two weeks late. The homeowner hasn't asked about timing yet.
What do you do?

options.text: Sign first, then mention the delay once work starts
options.feedback: You keep the job today. But the homeowner will feel tricked, and in home services most new work comes from referrals and reviews.

options.text: Tell them now and offer options, like other cabinets or a revised schedule
options.feedback: You might lose this job or some margin. You gain a client who believes your next quote, and tells neighbors.

options.text: Quietly add two weeks to the schedule without explaining why
options.feedback: Nothing you say is false, and the date will hold. But you miss the chance to show the client you put their interests first.

cards.title: Your word negotiates before you do.
body: Every honest deal lowers the cost of the next one. Every caught lie raises it.
**Try it today:** think of your last tough negotiation. Write down what the other side asked you to prove or guarantee. How much of that was the trust tax?
